h1: Investor Renovation Contractor in New Orleans
intro: Renovating in New Orleans is its own discipline. A shotgun double in Bywater, a raised basement house in Gentilly and a post-Katrina slab rebuild in Lakeview share a ZIP code prefix and almost nothing else: different foundations, different flood exposure, different historic review, different buyer. Old-growth cypress and heart pine framing can last for generations or be quietly hollowed out by Formosan termites, and the only way to know is to open it up. Genstone Construction works with flippers, BRRRR and rental investors, owners of doubles and fourplexes, FHA 203(k) buyers and REO asset managers across Orleans Parish and the surrounding parishes. We coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors, and a designated field manager runs your project from the first walk-through to final billing. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review tests repairs, flood exposure, historic district limits and ARV before you commit. From there you get a line-item scope and draw schedule, permits and HDLC paperwork handled, progress documentation you can follow from anywhere, and no upfront payment.
housingStock:
New Orleans has one of the deepest stocks of nineteenth- and early twentieth-century wood houses in the country, and most investor deals involve them. The older riverfront neighborhoods, including the Marigny, Bywater, Treme, the Seventh Ward, St. Roch, Holy Cross and the Irish Channel, are dense with Creole cottages, shotgun singles and doubles, camelbacks and side-hall houses. Many were built of old-growth cypress and longleaf heart pine on brick piers, with tall ceilings, plaster or beadboard walls, transoms and wood floors. That material is durable and valuable when it is sound, and a scope should preserve it wherever possible.

Moving away from the river, Mid-City, Broadmoor, Carrollton and parts of Gentilly fill in with early twentieth-century shotguns, California-style bungalows and raised basement houses, where the main living floor sits a full story up over a ground-level space that was often later enclosed. Gentilly and Lakeview also have brick and frame houses from the 1940s and 1950s, many of which flooded in 2005 and were gutted, raised or replaced. New Orleans East is mostly slab-on-grade ranch houses from the 1960s through the 1980s, a very different renovation from anything in the older city.

The ground underneath it all is soft. Much of the city sits on former marsh and swamp soils that compress over time, so pier houses settle unevenly and need periodic releveling, while slab houses can crack and tilt. Add the age of the stock and you should expect lead paint on almost everything built before 1978, knob-and-tube wiring in older houses that never had a full rewire, cast-iron and clay sewer laterals, and asbestos in some mid-century siding, flooring and duct wrap. A New Orleans rehab budget that does not account for leveling, termite repair and wiring is incomplete.

commonIssues.title: Settlement and releveling
commonIssues.body: Soft soils and brick pier foundations mean many New Orleans houses are out of level, sometimes dramatically. Symptoms include sloping floors, doors that swing open on their own, cracked plaster at door corners and gaps under baseboards. Releveling, sometimes called house leveling or shoring, involves jacking the house and resetting or rebuilding piers, and it should happen before plaster repair, trim, tile and cabinets. We have a qualified leveling contractor evaluate the house early so the cost is in your offer, not in a change order.

commonIssues.title: Formosan termite damage
commonIssues.body: New Orleans has one of the heaviest Formosan termite populations in the United States. Colonies are large, they nest in wet wood above ground as well as in soil, and they swarm in late spring. In older houses, damage hides in sills, joists, wall studs, door frames and even roof framing near leaks. We open suspect areas early, coordinate treatment with a licensed pest control company and price framing repairs on separate scope lines so you can see the true cost of the house.

commonIssues.title: Old wiring and plumbing
commonIssues.body: Knob-and-tube wiring is still found in older New Orleans houses, often mixed with later circuits added in stages. Insurers and buyers' lenders tend to push back on it. Plumbing can include galvanized supply lines, cast-iron drains and clay or cast-iron sewer laterals to the street, which can be damaged by settlement and tree roots. A rewire and a sewer camera inspection are often among the first scope items we recommend before finishes are priced.

commonIssues.title: Water intrusion and flood history
commonIssues.body: Between heavy rains, street flooding, roof leaks and the history of 2005, water is the main enemy of New Orleans houses. Investors find rotten sills, mold behind drywall, buckled floors and enclosed ground floors in raised basement houses that flood repeatedly. We check flood zone, elevation and any past flood claims during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review, use moisture meters and open walls where needed, and price drainage, roof and remediation work before cosmetic items.

commonIssues.title: Unpermitted past work
commonIssues.body: Many New Orleans houses have been altered over decades, including doubles converted to singles and back, ground floors enclosed for living space, and additions or camelbacks built without permits. Those changes can create problems with zoning, unit count, flood compliance and historic review. We look for signs of unpermitted work, check permit history where available, and plan the scope so the house ends up with a clear record that a buyer, lender or insurer will accept.

investorMarket:
New Orleans investment strategy depends heavily on elevation, historic district status and the buyer pool. The older riverfront neighborhoods, sometimes called the sliver by the river, sit on higher ground and draw owner-occupant buyers who want original character. Flips there succeed when the work respects the house: preserved cypress and heart pine, restored millwork, and modern kitchens and baths fitted into historic floor plans. HDLC review in local historic districts affects what can be changed outside, so plan for it.

Doubles are central to the rental market. Shotgun doubles throughout Mid-City, Central City, the Seventh Ward and Uptown can be renovated as two rental units, converted to a single-family house for resale, or occupied by an owner on one side with a tenant on the other. Each path has different zoning, permit and financing considerations.

Gentilly, Broadmoor and parts of Mid-City offer raised basement and bungalow-style houses that appeal to families and FHA 203(k) buyers. New Orleans East and parts of Algiers carry slab ranch houses that suit buy-and-hold investors looking for simpler renovations. Across the city, insurance cost has become a major factor in deals. Roof age and construction, wind mitigation and flood exposure can swing the carrying cost enough to change whether a hold makes sense. Short-term rental rules are tight in most residential areas, so we recommend underwriting long-term rental income unless your specific property and permits clearly support another use. The Pre-Offer Rehab Review puts these factors next to the repair estimate before you commit.
permits:
Permits in New Orleans are issued by the City of New Orleans Department of Safety and Permits, which covers building, electrical, plumbing and mechanical work and coordinates inspections. Structural work, releveling, roofing, electrical and plumbing changes, HVAC replacement, window and door changes, additions and conversions between unit counts all typically require permits. Zoning questions, including unit counts on doubles, fall under the city's comprehensive zoning ordinance and the City Planning Commission.

Historic review is a major factor. Properties in local historic districts, which include large parts of the Marigny, Bywater, Treme, Holy Cross, the Irish Channel and other older neighborhoods, need approval from the Historic District Landmarks Commission for many exterior changes, including windows, doors, siding, porches, roofing and demolition. French Quarter properties fall under the Vieux Carré Commission. Plan time for that review in your schedule.

Louisiana requires contractors to be licensed or registered with the Louisiana State Licensing Board for Contractors for residential construction and home improvement work above set thresholds. Water and sewer connections involve the Sewerage and Water Board. Genstone coordinates licensed local trades, prepares permit and HDLC submissions, schedules inspections and collects lien waivers with every draw.
climate:
New Orleans has a hot, humid subtropical climate with heavy rainfall spread through the year and a hurricane season that runs from early summer through fall. Hurricane Ida in 2021 damaged roofs across the region, and many houses still carry patched roofs and decking from that and earlier storms. We sequence roof work and dry-in early on any project that will run into storm season, and we secure materials when a storm approaches.

Intense summer downpours can overwhelm street drainage, so low-lying lots and enclosed ground floors flood more often than flood maps suggest. Humidity keeps mold and Formosan termites active, and closed, unconditioned houses deteriorate quickly. Interior work like plaster repair, wood flooring and painting needs climate control to cure properly. Hard freezes are rare but do happen, and pipes under raised houses are exposed, so insulating supply lines in crawlspaces is a practical part of most scopes.

faqs.q: Does my New Orleans renovation need HDLC approval?
faqs.a: If the property is in a local historic district or is a designated landmark, many exterior changes require Historic District Landmarks Commission approval. That usually includes windows, doors, siding, porches, roofing materials and demolition. Interior work generally does not need HDLC review. We check district status during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review, prepare the submission with photos and specifications, and schedule exterior work around the approval so it does not hold up the rest of the project.

faqs.q: How do you handle releveling on a shotgun or Creole cottage?
faqs.a: A qualified leveling contractor evaluates the house and recommends how many piers to reset or rebuild and how far to raise the low points. Releveling is done before plaster repair, trim, tile and cabinets, because lifting the house moves everything above it. We price it as its own line in the scope with its own draw. Where termite damage or rot is found in sills and joists during leveling, those repairs are priced and documented as well.

faqs.q: Do you work outside Orleans Parish?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone coordinates vetted, licensed local contractors in Metairie, Kenner, Chalmette, Arabi, Gretna, Harvey, Westwego and other parts of the metro. Jefferson and St. Bernard parishes have their own permit offices and inspection procedures, and the housing stock differs, with more slab ranch houses in many suburban areas. Your field manager handles permits in the correct jurisdiction and notes any parish-specific requirements in the scope.

faqs.q: Can I manage a New Orleans renovation from out of state?
faqs.a: Yes. Many of our clients invest remotely. Your designated field manager coordinates local trades, handles permits and HDLC paperwork, and documents progress with photos and milestone updates you can review without traveling. Draws are released only for completed work, and the final payment follows your approval of the finished house. You stay involved in decisions without needing to be on site for each one.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in New Orleans, LA | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: New Orleans fix and flip renovations that respect cypress shotguns and Creole cottages, with releveling, rewiring, HDLC review and roof work scoped up front.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in New Orleans
fix-flip.intro: New Orleans buyers will pay for a renovated shotgun or Creole cottage, but they are knowledgeable, and they can tell restored from stripped. Exposed cypress, original heart pine floors, tall doors and transoms carry real value here, while gray vinyl, cheap trim and a level-looking floor that is actually floating on failing piers can sink a sale at inspection. Genstone builds New Orleans flip scopes from the piers up. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review checks leveling, termite damage, wiring, roof condition, flood exposure and historic district status alongside your comps and ARV. The resulting scope lists labor, materials and a draw schedule, often with more than one finish plan. A designated field manager coordinates licensed local trades, handles permits and HDLC paperwork, and keeps the project moving to protect your carrying costs.

sections.h2: Structure first: leveling, termites and rewiring
sections.body:
Most New Orleans flips that lose money do it in the structure, not the finishes. A buyer's inspector will check floors with a level, look under the house at the piers, probe sills for termite damage and open the panel. If they find a house that was finished over settlement, active Formosan damage or knob-and-tube wiring, the deal turns into a negotiation, and the buyer's insurer may refuse to write a policy at all.

So we put structure and systems at the top of the scope. A leveling contractor evaluates the piers and recommends the work. Suspect wood is probed and opened so termite damage can be priced and repaired before walls are closed. Wiring is evaluated, and in most older houses, a full rewire with a new panel is the cleanest answer. The sewer lateral is scoped with a camera. Only then do we price plaster, trim, floors, kitchens and baths. The result is a house that inspects cleanly, a stack of documentation you can hand to the buyer's agent, and a listing price that holds.

sections.h2: Finishes that suit the neighborhood and the house
sections.body:
Buyers shopping Bywater, the Marigny, the Irish Channel or Holy Cross want the house's history to show. That means refinishing original pine floors where they survive, keeping or restoring tall interior doors and transoms, repairing plaster or beadboard rather than covering it, and preserving fireplaces and mantels even when they are decorative. Kitchens and baths can be modern, but they should feel like they belong in the house. Opening a shotgun's rooms completely can backfire with buyers who like its proportions, so we look at what nearby renovated comps actually did.

In Gentilly, Broadmoor and parts of Mid-City, buyers often want more open, family-friendly layouts in bungalows and raised basement houses, plus a clear answer on flood history. Lakeview buyers compare your flip with recently rebuilt or raised houses, so finishes and systems need to meet that standard. In each case, we can prepare more than one finish plan so you can compare cost against the ARV and choose the level the comps support.

Two outside schedules affect New Orleans flips: historic review and the weather. In local historic districts, exterior changes like windows, doors, siding, porches and roofing generally need Historic District Landmarks Commission approval. We prepare the submission early, with photos and specifications, so exterior work is approved by the time interior work is wrapping up. Replacing original wood windows with vinyl is usually not approved in those districts, so we plan for repairing original windows or installing appropriate replacements.

Hurricane season brings a different risk. A house with an open roof or missing windows in late summer is exposed. On projects running into storm season, we prioritize roofing and dry-in, secure materials when a storm approaches, and document the house's condition before and after. After a regional storm, contractors get booked quickly, which can slow your project, so getting the roof done early is a practical hedge. Your field manager tracks both schedules and keeps you updated.

faqs.q: Should I keep original features in a New Orleans flip?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Buyers in the historic neighborhoods pay attention to cypress and heart pine floors, tall doors, transoms, mantels and plaster. Preserving them often costs less than replacing them with new materials and typically supports a stronger sale. Where original features are too damaged, we look for replacements that match the house. We can price alternatives so you can see the cost difference before deciding what to do.

faqs.q: How much does HDLC review affect a flip schedule?
faqs.a: It depends on the scope. Interior work does not need HDLC approval, and many exterior repairs that replace in kind are simpler to approve. Changes to windows, doors, porches, siding or roofing materials take more review. We submit early so exterior work is approved while interior work is happening, which helps keep the overall schedule on track for your New Orleans listing.

faqs.q: Will buyers ask about flood history on my flip?
faqs.a: Yes, especially in Gentilly, Lakeview, Broadmoor and other areas that flooded in 2005. Buyers and their lenders look at flood zone, elevation and any past claims, and insurance quotes depend on them. We check that information during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review and document drainage, roof and moisture work so you can answer those questions clearly when your New Orleans house goes on the market.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in New Orleans, LA | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: New Orleans BRRRR renovations for doubles, shotguns and ranch houses: appraisal-ready work, insurable roofs and wiring, and durable rental finishes.
brrrr.intro: The classic New Orleans BRRRR deal is a shotgun double bought tired and renovated into two solid rental units, but single shotguns, Gentilly bungalows and New Orleans East ranch houses all fit the strategy too. What makes or breaks the refinance here is often not the kitchen. It is whether the roof, wiring and structure support a reasonable insurance quote and a clean appraisal. Genstone writes BRRRR scopes for both ends of the deal: work the appraiser can credit and the insurer can accept, built with materials that stand up to humidity, termites and years of tenants. We start with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review covering repairs, ARV and insurance-sensitive items. Then a designated field manager coordinates licensed local trades and permits, and Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans if you want the refinance handled within the Genstone Companies.

sections.h2: Insurance can make or break the refinance
sections.body:
Louisiana's insurance market has been difficult since the hurricanes of 2020 and 2021, and in New Orleans the premium on a rental can significantly affect DSCR math. Lenders look at that expense when sizing the refinance, so a house that appraises well but carries a high premium may not cash out the way you planned.

The items insurers look at most closely are the roof, the electrical system, plumbing and the structure. A new roof built to current wind standards with sealed decking, a full rewire that removes knob-and-tube, updated plumbing and a level, termite-free structure all tend to help. Louisiana has also offered grants through its Fortify Homes Program for roofs built to the FORTIFIED standard; availability changes, so check the current program before counting on it. We price these items in your scope and gather the documentation an insurer or lender will want, including roof specifications, permits and inspection results. That puts you in a better position when you shop the policy before the refinance.

Shotgun doubles are a staple of New Orleans BRRRR investing because they offer two rents on one lot. Before buying, confirm that the property is legally a two-unit building under current zoning and that both units have the separate meters and services you plan to rely on. Doubles that were converted to singles and back over the years can have unclear status, which affects both permits and the appraisal.

For the renovation, we treat the shared components, including the roof, foundation piers, sewer lateral and electrical service, as building-level items and price them separately from each unit's interior. Appraisers value doubles using rental income and comparable sales, so both units need to be in strong, consistent condition. An updated kitchen and bath in each unit, durable flooring, new or well-maintained HVAC, and visible structural and systems work all support the valuation. We provide a completed-work summary with permits and photos that you can hand to the appraiser at the inspection.

sections.h2: Rental finishes built for heat, humidity and termites
sections.body:
After the refinance, the house has to perform for years. In New Orleans, that means choosing materials that handle humidity and discourage termites. We favor waterproof flooring in kitchens, baths and high-traffic areas, while refinishing original pine floors in living spaces where they are sound, because they are durable and tenants value them. Bathrooms get moisture-resistant walls and exhaust fans vented outdoors.

Outside and underneath, we focus on keeping water away from wood. That means gutters and downspouts that discharge away from the piers, repairing rotted siding and trim, and making sure the crawlspace can dry out. Formosan termites are drawn to wet wood, so fixing leaks quickly and maintaining a treatment plan protects your investment. HVAC needs to keep up with long, humid summers, and mini-split systems can work well in shotguns without existing ductwork. Our one-year workmanship warranty covers the renovation; tenant damage and normal wear are not included.

faqs.q: Is a shotgun double a good BRRRR property in New Orleans?
faqs.a: It can be, because it offers two rents on one lot. The key is confirming legal two-unit status, separate utilities, and the condition of shared components like the roof, piers and sewer line. Insurance costs also matter for the refinance. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review evaluates repairs and insurance-sensitive items alongside the expected after-repair value so you can test the deal first.

faqs.q: What repairs help a New Orleans rental get insured?
faqs.a: Insurers commonly focus on roof age and construction, electrical systems, plumbing and overall structural condition. A new roof, a full rewire, updated plumbing and documented releveling and termite repairs typically help. We include these items in the scope and provide specifications and permits, but insurance decisions are made by the carrier, so talk with your agent early in the process.

faqs.q: Can Genstone Financial handle the BRRRR refinance?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans along with fix-and-flip loans, lines of credit and new construction loans. Using it is optional. If you have your own lender, we provide the scope, draw records and completion documentation they need. Genstone Property Management can also lease and manage the New Orleans property after the renovation if you want, which keeps the handoff from rehab to tenant in one set of hands.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in New Orleans | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Single-family rental renovation in New Orleans: termite, moisture and wiring work, durable finishes and fast, documented turns for shotguns and ranches.
rental-renovation.h1: Single-Family Rental Renovations in New Orleans
rental-renovation.intro: A New Orleans rental portfolio rarely looks uniform. One owner might hold a single shotgun in Mid-City, a raised basement house in Gentilly, a bungalow in Broadmoor and a slab ranch in New Orleans East, each with its own foundation, wiring and moisture problems. Genstone renovates and turns single-family rentals for individual landlords, funds and institutional owners across Orleans Parish and nearby areas. We write a portfolio standard that works across those house types, coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors, and handle permits and inspections with the city. A designated field manager documents each property with photos and completion records, and Genstone Field Services can handle inspections, occupied maintenance and turn and make-ready work between full renovations, so you can keep the portfolio in good shape without being on site.

sections.h2: One standard for very different houses
sections.body:
Writing a rental standard for New Orleans means accounting for houses built a century apart. Our standard defines the outcome rather than forcing identical products into every house: water-resistant flooring where moisture is likely, refinished wood floors where originals are sound, washable paint in consistent colors, solid cabinets, durable counters and fixtures with parts available locally.

Systems standards are just as important. Older pier houses get evaluated for releveling, termite damage, knob-and-tube wiring and sewer lateral condition. Raised basement houses get a close look at the lower level, which may flood in heavy rain, so we avoid finishing it with materials that will be ruined by water. Slab ranches in New Orleans East need attention to plumbing under the slab and HVAC sizing. Across all of them, we require working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, GFCI protection where code calls for it, and secure doors and windows. Consistency reduces maintenance costs and makes each new acquisition easier to price.

sections.h2: Keeping water and termites out of rentals
sections.body:
In New Orleans, the biggest long-term threats to a rental are water and Formosan termites, and the two are connected. Termites favor wet wood, so a slow leak under a sink, around a tub or at a roof penetration can become a nesting site. A rental that is not watched for leaks can suffer serious structural damage before a tenant reports anything.

We build water management into every rental scope. Roofs, flashing and gutters are repaired or replaced, downspouts discharge away from piers and foundations, crawlspaces are checked for standing water, and plumbing leaks are fixed rather than patched. At each turn, we inspect the usual trouble spots and look for mud tubes, swarmer wings and soft wood. When we find activity, we document it, coordinate treatment with a licensed pest control company, and price the repair. Catching problems during routine work costs far less than replacing sills and joists later, and it keeps the house insurable.

Vacancy costs New Orleans landlords more than most repairs. Genstone runs turns as a repeatable process. After move-out, a field inspection documents condition with photos and produces a scope based on your standard, separating tenant damage from normal wear so security deposit decisions are clear.

Trades are scheduled in order, so patching and painting come before flooring and final cleaning, and plumbing and electrical checks happen before anything is closed up. Each turn is also a chance to check for signs of settlement, leaks and termites before they become emergencies. In older houses, we pay attention to lead-safe work practices whenever painted surfaces are disturbed, because most of the city's rental stock was built before 1978. You approve the scope, follow progress through photos, and pay only for completed work. The completion record gives you a clear baseline for the next lease and documentation if questions come up with a tenant or insurer.

faqs.q: Do you handle rental turns in New Orleans?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone handles full renovations and recurring turns, and Genstone Field Services can provide make-ready work, inspections and occupied maintenance between larger projects. Each turn starts with a documented inspection and a scope based on your portfolio standard. You approve the work, track progress remotely and pay for completed work. The goal is a clean, safe house ready for the next tenant without unnecessary vacancy.

faqs.q: How do you deal with lead paint in older New Orleans rentals?
faqs.a: Most of the city's rental housing was built before 1978, so we assume painted surfaces may contain lead unless testing shows otherwise. Work that disturbs paint is done using lead-safe practices, with containment and cleanup. Landlords also have disclosure duties for pre-1978 housing. We include lead-safe work in the scope where needed and document it as part of the completion record.

faqs.q: Can you manage rentals across Orleans and Jefferson parishes?
faqs.a: Yes. We coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors in New Orleans, Metairie, Kenner, Gretna, Harvey and other parts of the metro, and handle permits in each parish. Suburban houses are often slab ranches with different needs than older city houses, and the scope reflects that. Your field manager provides documentation for each property so you can manage the portfolio as a whole.

multifamily-renovation.title: Shotgun Double & 2–4 Unit Renovation in New Orleans
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Shotgun doubles, camelbacks and fourplexes in New Orleans renovated around tenants: shared piers, roofs, sewer and wiring, with zoning and HDLC handled.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Shotgun Double and Small Multifamily Renovation in New Orleans
multifamily-renovation.intro: Small multifamily in New Orleans mostly means the shotgun double: two long, narrow units side by side under one roof, often with a camelback rising over the rear rooms. You also find side-hall doubles, early twentieth-century fourplexes in Mid-City and Uptown, and larger old houses divided into apartments. These buildings carry a lot of the city's rental housing, and they come with shared piers, roofs, sewer laterals and, sometimes, unclear unit status. Genstone renovates 2–4 unit buildings for investors who want higher rents, lower operating costs, a value-add refinance or a conversion strategy. We plan work around occupied units, coordinate vetted, licensed local trades, and handle permits, zoning questions and HDLC review where needed. A designated field manager keeps the project documented from start to finish.

sections.body:
In a shotgun double, the two units share a roof, a center party wall, a foundation of brick piers and usually a sewer lateral to the street. When the house settles, both units' doors and floors go out of level together. When the roof leaks at the ridge, water can end up on either side. When termites reach the center wall framing, both units are affected. That means building-level work needs to come first and be priced separately from interiors.

We start with a releveling evaluation and pier repair, then look at the roof, the party wall framing and the sewer line. The electrical service matters too: many doubles have separate meters, but older services may be undersized or partially rewired. Fire separation between units is checked, and smoke and carbon monoxide detection is brought up to current expectations. Once the building is sound, we scope each unit's interior. Listing building-level items separately makes it easier to compare costs with the rent increase and decide what can wait.

sections.h2: Keeping, converting or splitting a double
sections.body:
Investors in New Orleans often choose between keeping a double as two rental units, converting it to a single-family house for resale, or living in one side and renting the other. Each option affects permits, zoning, financing and the scope. Converting a double to a single usually means removing a kitchen, opening the center wall in places, and consolidating utilities, and buyers in neighborhoods like Bywater and the Irish Channel may pay for the space. Keeping it as a double preserves rental income and may suit a BRRRR or long-term hold.

Before committing to a plan, confirm the legal unit count and the zoning rules that apply, because some doubles have been converted back and forth without permits. In historic districts, exterior changes such as removing a front door or altering a porch can require HDLC approval. We help you compare the options during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so your offer reflects the path you intend to take.

Many small multifamily purchases in New Orleans come with tenants in one or more units. We phase the work so vacant units get the full interior renovation first and occupied units are handled at lease turnover or through agreed access windows. Building-level work like the roof, exterior paint, gutters and porch repair can usually proceed without entering units.

Releveling an occupied double needs extra care, because lifting the building can shift doors, crack plaster and disturb plumbing on both sides. We coordinate it with tenants, protect their belongings, and follow up with any needed adjustments. Utility shutoffs for sewer, water or electrical work are scheduled and announced in advance. Air conditioning is essential in a New Orleans summer, so HVAC work is completed as quickly as possible. Lead-safe practices apply in pre-1978 buildings, and we use containment to protect tenants. Your field manager coordinates schedules with you or your property manager so everyone knows what to expect.

faqs.q: Can you relevel a shotgun double with tenants living in it?
faqs.a: Often, yes, with careful planning. Releveling affects both units, so tenants need notice, belongings near walls should be protected, and doors and plumbing may need adjustment afterward. We coordinate the work with you or your property manager and schedule it to minimize disruption. In some cases, it makes sense to wait until one side is vacant before doing the work.

faqs.q: Should I convert a New Orleans double into a single-family house?
faqs.a: It depends on the neighborhood, zoning and your strategy. In some areas, renovated singles sell well to owner-occupants, while in others two rental units produce stronger returns. Conversion requires permits and may require HDLC approval for exterior changes. We can price both options during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so you can compare them before buying. Owner-occupants sometimes keep the double and live on one side, which is a third path worth pricing.

faqs.q: What should I check before buying a fourplex in Mid-City or Uptown?
faqs.a: Confirm the legal unit count and zoning, then look at the foundation, roof, electrical service and metering, sewer line, fire separation and smoke and carbon monoxide detection. Check for termite damage and signs of past water intrusion. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review evaluates these items and estimates repairs so you can compare them with the expected rents before making an offer.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in New Orleans, LA | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor for New Orleans buyers and agents: bids for releveling, termite repair, rewiring and roofs on older shotguns and bungalows.
fha-203k.h1: FHA 203(k) Renovation Contractor in New Orleans
fha-203k.intro: Many New Orleans houses that buyers fall for are not financeable as-is. The floors slope, the wiring is decades old, the roof was patched after the last storm, and there is soft wood around the back steps. An FHA 203(k) loan lets an owner-occupant buyer finance the purchase and the repairs together, which can make an older shotgun, Creole cottage or Gentilly bungalow realistic. As an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor, Genstone Construction works with buyers, agents, lenders and 203(k) consultants to prepare detailed bids that fit the program and the house, including the releveling, termite and wiring work common here. After closing, a designated field manager coordinates vetted, licensed local trades, handles permits and HDLC review where needed, and documents each draw.

sections.h2: Why most older New Orleans houses need a Standard 203(k)
sections.body:
The Limited 203(k) is meant for non-structural repairs and is capped at $75,000. It can work for a structurally sound house that needs a roof, HVAC, electrical and plumbing updates, flooring, paint, and kitchen or bath work, such as a slab ranch in New Orleans East or a well-maintained bungalow.

Many older New Orleans houses, though, need releveling, pier repair or replacement of termite-damaged framing, which are structural repairs. Those require the Standard 203(k), which involves a HUD-approved 203(k) consultant. The program's minimum repair amount is $5,000. We help buyers and agents identify which loan type fits the house during the initial walk-through. Getting that right early matters, because switching from Limited to Standard after an inspection uncovers structural issues can disrupt the closing schedule. We also flag houses with flood exposure or unclear unit status that could complicate financing so the buyer can make an informed decision before the inspection period runs out.

sections.h2: Good and difficult 203(k) houses in New Orleans
sections.body:
Good candidates usually have a sound overall structure with clear, fixable issues. A Gentilly raised basement house that needs a roof, HVAC, rewiring and a kitchen and bath update is a common example. So is a Mid-City shotgun that needs releveling, termite repairs, a rewire and new plumbing, financed through a Standard 203(k) with a consultant. Slab ranches in New Orleans East and Algiers with dated systems and finishes often fit a Limited 203(k).

Difficult cases include houses with severe structural damage, extensive water damage or uncertain flood compliance, and doubles or conversions where the legal unit count is unclear. They are not always impossible, but they require careful evaluation. Houses in historic districts can still work well with a 203(k), but exterior changes may need HDLC approval, which should be planned into the renovation schedule. Lead paint rules apply to most of the city's older housing and affect how painted surfaces are handled.

A 203(k) bid has to satisfy several readers: the lender's underwriter, the consultant on Standard loans, and the buyer who needs to understand what they are paying for. Our bids break out labor and materials by trade, describe each item clearly, and include a draw schedule tied to completed work. On Standard loans, we coordinate with the consultant so our bid and their work write-up match before submission.

After closing, the work proceeds in stages. Releveling and structural repair typically come first, followed by systems, then finishes. Each draw request includes photos and completion documentation, and the consultant or lender inspection confirms the work before funds are released. Your field manager handles permits with the Department of Safety and Permits and coordinates HDLC approval where needed so approvals arrive in time for each draw. Buyers pay nothing upfront, and the final payment follows completion and approval. Agents on both sides receive updates, so nobody is guessing where the renovation stands when the buyer calls.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) loan cover releveling a New Orleans house?
faqs.a: Yes, but releveling is structural, so it typically requires a Standard 203(k) with a HUD-approved consultant. We coordinate with the leveling contractor and the consultant so the work is clearly described in the bid and appears in the draw schedule. Termite damage found during leveling can be addressed in the same scope if it is identified and priced. Opening suspect areas before closing reduces the chance of a mid-project change order.

faqs.q: Are historic district houses eligible for 203(k) financing?
faqs.a: Yes. Many houses in New Orleans historic districts are financed with 203(k) loans. The difference is that exterior changes like windows, doors, siding, porches and roofing materials may need Historic District Landmarks Commission approval. We plan that review into the renovation schedule so it does not delay draws or the completion of the work. Repairing original features in kind is usually the simplest path through review in a 203(k) project.

faqs.q: Is Genstone a certified 203(k) contractor in New Orleans?
faqs.a: It is. Genstone carries FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor status, and we prepare bids for lenders and consultants, coordinate vetted, licensed local trades in the New Orleans area, and document each draw. The lender makes final decisions on the loan and the contractor, so check with your loan officer early and bring us in when you have a target house. A walk-through before the offer lets us flag structural items that point toward the Standard version.

reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in New Orleans
reo-renovation.intro: Vacant houses in New Orleans decline quickly. Humidity feeds mold, roof leaks feed Formosan termites, vines and overgrowth take over yards and porches, and an unsecured house can attract squatters or theft. The city also pursues blighted and neglected properties through code enforcement, so a bank-owned house left alone can pick up citations, fines and liens. Genstone works with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises, for which we are a preferred contractor, to secure, stabilize and renovate REO properties across Orleans Parish and the surrounding parishes. Genstone Field Services handles property preservation, inspections and code compliance, while our renovation team prices and completes repairs through vetted, licensed local trades. Every step is documented with photos, condition reports, lien waivers and completion records for asset managers and investor reporting.

sections.h2: Blight enforcement and vacant property care
sections.body:
New Orleans takes blight seriously. The city's code enforcement process can bring inspections, hearings, fines and liens against neglected properties, and a bank-owned house with an overgrown yard, broken windows or a damaged roof can draw attention quickly. Once a case is open, it needs a documented response.

Genstone Field Services handles the preservation work that keeps properties compliant: securing doors and windows, boarding where necessary, removing trash and debris, cutting grass and clearing vines and overgrowth, and making sure the exterior does not deteriorate further. When the city issues a notice, we track it, complete the required work, document it with photos, and coordinate any reinspection. Where permitted work is needed, such as roof replacement or structural repair, our field manager pulls the permits with the Department of Safety and Permits. In historic districts, demolition by neglect and exterior repairs can also involve the Historic District Landmarks Commission, so we plan for that review when needed.

sections.h2: What vacancy does to New Orleans houses
sections.body:
Without regular attention, a vacant New Orleans house can lose a lot of value in a single season. Humidity builds inside when the power and air conditioning are off, and mold spreads across drywall, plaster and wood. Roof leaks, especially on roofs patched after past storms, let water reach framing, where Formosan termites take advantage. Gutters clog, porches rot and vines can damage siding.

Our first inspection documents conditions with photos and a written report. We identify immediate hazards, active leaks, mold, termite activity, settlement, theft of HVAC equipment or copper, and signs of unauthorized entry. Emergency items such as roof leaks and open entries are separated from the full repair list so asset managers can approve urgent work quickly. That documentation also supports insurance claims for damage that occurred during the holding period, and it gives the asset manager a clear basis for deciding whether to sell as-is or invest in repairs.

The right repair scope for a New Orleans REO depends on where the property is going. A house in a historic neighborhood headed to owner-occupant buyers may justify releveling, termite repair, a new roof and rewiring so it can qualify for financing and insurance. A property headed to investors may sell best with safety, code and weatherproofing items addressed and the rest left to the buyer.

We typically price several options so asset managers can compare them with broker price opinions and expected recovery. Each scope includes labor, materials, debris removal and dumpsters, organized by priority: safety and code, weatherproofing, structure and systems, then cosmetic work. We document every completed task with photos and collect lien waivers and contractor compliance paperwork with each payment. If a buyer's inspection finds something new, the same field manager can price and complete the repair, which keeps the file moving toward closing. Roof and termite documentation is kept in the file because New Orleans buyers and their insurers almost always ask for it.

faqs.q: Can you respond to a New Orleans blight notice on a bank-owned property?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone Field Services can complete the cleanup, securing, overgrowth removal and exterior repairs needed to address a notice, document the work with photos, and coordinate any reinspection. Where permits are required, our field manager pulls them with the Department of Safety and Permits. In historic districts, we also plan for any Historic District Landmarks Commission review needed for exterior work.

faqs.q: What damage is most common in vacant New Orleans houses?
faqs.a: Mold, roof leaks, Formosan termite damage, rotted porches and siding, settlement, overgrowth and theft of HVAC equipment or copper are all common. Our first inspection documents each issue with photos and separates emergency items, such as active leaks and open entries, from the full repair list so the asset manager can approve urgent work quickly. In humid months, a short delay on a roof leak can turn into a much larger mold and termite repair.

faqs.q: Do you work with servicers and GSEs on New Orleans REO files?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone works with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and other lenders, and is a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises. We provide photos, condition reports, repair options, lien waivers and completion records so files are well documented. Genstone Field Services also handles preservation, inspections and code compliance, so a single team carries the property from first secure through repairs and on to closing in Orleans Parish or the surrounding parishes.
